organizations.name: Taliban
organizations.notes: Led by Hibatullah Akhundzada. Hosts say it needs no Russian bounties to attack Americans and claims its attacks officially. It signed the US withdrawal deal on 29 Feb 2020. Voice of Jihad is its website.

organizations.name: GRU
organizations.notes: A GRU unit was reported by the New York Times to have offered bounties to Taliban-linked actors to kill US soldiers.

organizations.name: al-Qaeda
organizations.notes: Hosts argue it is not solely Arab and publishes in Urdu and Pashto, with leadership drawn from Afghans and Pakistanis. It conceals its Afghan operations partly by publishing in Urdu.

organizations.name: Islamic State
organizations.notes: A spin-off of al-Qaeda. Hosts say Pakistan's tolerance of the Taliban created a permissive environment for its rise. It attacked Americans and Russia.

organizations.name: Islamic Caucasus Emirate
organizations.notes: Described as an al-Qaeda branch, probably defunct after Russian targeting of leaders and the ISIS challenge. It had a branch in Syria and carried out attacks in Moscow and St. Petersburg.

organizations.name: Katibat Imam al-Bukhari
organizations.notes: An Uzbek group that split from the IMU. Its emir in Syria posted photos claiming a joint raid with the Taliban in Afghanistan; the Taliban denied it.

organizations.name: Islamic Movement of Uzbekistan
organizations.notes: Parent group from which Katibat Imam al-Bukhari split.

organizations.name: Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps
organizations.notes: Linked to the Taliban through narcotics trafficking, with US designations cited.

organizations.name: Pakistani military and intelligence establishment
organizations.notes: Described as the Taliban's top state sponsor, giving safe haven, medical care, training, madrasas and recruiting centers, while receiving US aid.

organizations.name: Iran
organizations.notes: Ranked second Taliban sponsor, providing training camps, cash and safe haven. Also sponsors Shia militias in Iraq and reportedly offered bounties on US soldiers in Afghanistan (2010 report).

organizations.name: Qatar
organizations.notes: Hosts the Taliban political office in Doha and a permissive fundraising environment, and received the Taliban 5. Also hosts CENTCOM and a US base.

organizations.name: United Arab Emirates
organizations.notes: Reportedly competed with Qatar to host the Taliban political office.

organizations.name: Saudi Arabia
organizations.notes: Permissive of Taliban and Haqqani fundraising, with no known links to operations; it had a falling out with the Taliban over bin Laden.

organizations.name: Haqqani Network
organizations.notes: Mentioned as a beneficiary of fundraising networks in Saudi Arabia.

organizations.name: US Central Command
organizations.notes: Led by Gen. McKenzie, who said no attack had been linked to the Russian bounties; headquartered in part in Qatar.

organizations.name: Russian government
organizations.notes: Accused of offering bounties; hosted Taliban diplomatically and supplied some arms; supports Assad in Syria.

events.description: Suicide bomber hit Bagram while Vice President Cheney was visiting.
News report that Iran was paying bounties for American soldiers in Afghanistan.
The Taliban said they were not waging decades of jihad for a 'silly ministerial post'.
Bombing outside Bagram killed three Americans and wounded others. The Taliban claimed it as a suicide attack. It is the only attack cited as possibly Russian-bounty funded.
Taliban-claimed suicide bombing in Kabul killed an American, prompting Trump to temporarily suspend the talks.
Suicide bombing in or near Bagram, months after the April 2019 attack.
New York Times first reported that a GRU unit offered bounties to Taliban to kill Americans.
Gen. McKenzie said he saw no causative link between the bounties and any attack on US forces.
Hosts record the episode; congressional hearings on the Russian bounty story were held that week.

Imam al-Bukhari's Syria-based emir posted photos claiming a joint raid with the Taliban. Zabihullah Mujahid denied it as propaganda 'stolen from our archive', but it came from the emir's Telegram feed.
Imam Bukhari Battalion's emir in Syria posted photos of a joint raid with the Taliban to capture Afghans; Caleb Weiss reported it
Taliban spokesman Zabihullah Mujahid denied the report, calling it anti-peace propaganda stolen from Taliban archives, then released the 'original' photo
Turkestan Islamic Party claimed operations and published photos; Taliban denied as anti-peace propaganda
Pompeo said he had seen evidence the Taliban is working to destroy al-Qaeda in Afghanistan

key_claims: The Taliban has targeted Americans since 2001 and needs no Russian bounties; it claims its attacks through official channels, which argues against a criminal or bounty-funded operation in the April 2019 Bagram attack.
No specific attack has been causally linked to the alleged Russian bounties, and Gen. McKenzie said as much.

Pakistan is the Taliban's chief state sponsor, followed by Iran, then Qatar, with Russia placed between Qatar and Saudi Arabia, while Saudi Arabia and the UAE are mainly permissive for fundraising or hosting.
al-Qaeda is not solely an Arab organization, publishes heavily in Urdu and Pashto, and exploits the neglect of non-Arabic material to hide its operations in Afghanistan.
The Islamic Caucasus Emirate was effectively an al-Qaeda branch, closely linked to Afghanistan and Syria and not merely a nationalist Chechen movement.
Taliban leader Hibatullah Akhundzada sacrificed his own son in a suicide attack, which the hosts cite as evidence he is unlikely to compromise in peace talks.
The Taliban denies the presence of foreign jihadis in Afghanistan, as in its denial of the Imam al-Bukhari joint-raid photos, despite UN, US and its own propaganda confirming Uzbek fighters there.
The Imam Bukhari Battalion's photos of a joint raid with the Taliban came from its own Telegram feed, not stolen Taliban archives.
The Taliban's release of the 'original' photo inadvertently confirmed their ties to the Imam Bukhari Battalion.
The Taliban remain allied with foreign jihadist groups including the Imam Bukhari Battalion, the Turkestan Islamic Party and al-Qaeda, despite the Feb 29, 2020 deal.
The Taliban deny foreign jihadists' presence in order to protect the peace deal.
US government is not countering Taliban disinformation, leaving it to Long War Journal.
Pompeo's claim that the Taliban are working against al-Qaeda is unsubstantiated.
The Russian bounty story is a fragmentary and politicized intelligence leak that distorts the Afghan war picture.
